idiom_name: type Meters float64 + accessor conversion methods
implementation_notes: Go has no operator overloading and no units in the standard library, so the realization is one named type per unit with plain float64 arithmetic inside the type and conversion methods across types: type Meters float64, type Feet float64, constructors and Feet()/Meters() accessors. Because Go never converts between distinct named numeric types implicitly, adding a Meters to a Feet is a compile error - the type name carries the unit, which is the closest the language gets to units of measure. time.Duration is the standard-library precedent (a named int64 of nanoseconds with Seconds()/Hours() methods and explicit conversion at the boundaries), so for durations prefer Duration and its constants instead of inventing another type; untyped constants still adapt to the named type, so Meters(3) * 2 stays ergonomic.
pitfalls: A conversion that is really a cast - Meters(someFeetValue) - skips the factor and is indistinguishable from a correct call; keep one exported conversion per direction and review raw conversions.
The default %v form of a named float type prints a bare number, so logs and error messages lose the unit; implement String() and use it on every boundary.
json.Marshal/Unmarshal and database/sql see only the underlying float, so wire types must carry the unit explicitly or the receiver must know it out of band.

variants.name: martinlindhe/unit conversion library
variants.implementation_notes: When the unit catalogue should not be hand-written, github.com/martinlindhe/unit provides float64-based length, speed, mass and related types where a value is created by multiplying a unit constant (3 * unit.Kilometer) and read back through unit accessors such as .Meters() or .Feet(). It keeps the same Go shape - named types plus accessors, no operator overloading - but ships the factors and the dimension families, and it accepts your own underlying type by converting to the base unit first. Treat it as the default when a project needs more than a handful of units.
variants.code_sketch:
import "github.com/martinlindhe/unit"

span := 3 * unit.Kilometer
gap := 500 * unit.Meter
total := span.Add(gap)          // unit.Length, converted internally
fmt.Println(total.Meters())     // 3500
fmt.Println(total.Feet())       // 11482.9
pitfalls: The types alias float64 shares one underlying representation, so nothing stops a plain float from entering an expression - the discipline is to construct through unit constants.
Mixing dimensions still compiles where the library returns the same named type; check the returned type in wrappers rather than relying on the compiler.
